title: John Hammond's contribution to jazz
summary: After Bill Pemberton walks in, Jones calls Hammond the single force behind Granz, Wein, Gillespie and Charlie Parker's recognition, and Louis Armstrong's.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: There's the doorbell. Let's hold it. Keep that thought... We were interrupted by the doorbell and my old dear friend Bill Pemberton walked in and wants to sit in on the session.
Well you know how it is, into each rain a little life must fall.
So we'll excuse him for that. We were talking about John Hammond and his great interest and his great contribution to this American art form, jazz, in promoting Bessie Smith and you just name it.
I said, Milt, you know how our country was economically and socially, coming out of the 30's, Depression, and what have you. Somebody had to be here to keep the sweetening in the pot.

There is nobody that has been responsible, there has been no one single force, individual individual, that has been the force in order that you might have a Norman Granz, in order that you might have a George Wein, in order that you would ever know about a Fletcher Henderson, in order that you might know of anybody out here - there is not but one single force individually, not collectively, because the individuals fell by the wayside - than John Hammond. Without Mr. John Hammond you would not have the historical events that you have in the annals of jazz.
We wouldn't be sitting in a comfortable home for any jazz players, comfortable home.

Right. Now I'm covering a period. You would not have known about a Dizzy Gillespie. You wouldn't have known of a Charlie Parker. Do you understand? You wouldn't have known of a Jackie Paris. You wouldn't have known of a Looplegoop Seven. This man has offered us - who else? This man, he's an octopus. That's all I call him, he's an octopus.
What I wonder is why is it that people, the public, the general public in the world, don't really know this.

John has an - it's not an inferiority complex that he has. He realizes, you come in the world with nothing, you do nothing... And I can leave and go. You would never have a Benny Goodman story. You would not have had the magnitude of a fellow of the magnitude of Mr. Louis Armstrong unless there was John. He fought it, when they was writing it in the Down Beat in two paragraphs and Harry James took a trophy and threw it down. He said, "You'll never make a penny." "I don't care, the world's greatest jazz trumpet player is Mr. Louis Armstrong." They wrote of Mr. Armstrong in the Metronome and it came out like this.
Just a small column, is that what you're saying?
This, two inches of Pica... a Pica and a half... "Louis Armstrong did this" Oh YEAH?
